title: Chicago permit expediting firm (BACP-licensed) with AI-assisted application prep
product_service: Preparing, filing and shepherding City of Chicago building, sign and demolition permit applications (plan-based and express), correction responses, status tracking, fee payment and inspection scheduling; AI used to pre-check completeness, draft correction responses and monitor status.
target_customer: Small/mid developers, commercial tenants doing build-outs, retail/restaurant chains' construction managers, sign companies, condo associations, out-of-town GCs and architects who do not self-file.
purchase_motivation: Time-to-permit drives carrying cost and delayed rent/opening; DOB process complexity; out-of-town firms lack local process knowledge; architects/GCs offload clerical filing.
spending_evidence: 6,428 of 32,032 Chicago permits issued in 2025 listed an expediter contact, incl. 2,567 of 5,505 renovation/alteration and 424 of 1,460 new-construction permits [A, WS10-S010]; the Public Building Commission ran a dedicated permit-expediter RFP with task orders [B, WS10-S009].
representative_operators: 204 distinct individual expediters appear on 2025 Chicago permits; top 10 handled 46.3% of expediter-listed permits, 34 handled >=50 each, the busiest 969 [A, WS10-S010]
revenue_mechanism: Per-permit flat fee by complexity plus hourly for corrections/meetings; City permit fees passed through; retainers for repeat filers.
typical_transaction_value: Private-market fee MISSING; one public-owner task order capped basic application services at $350 (2018) [B, WS10-S009]; hypothesis $500-$3,000 per plan-based permit [E].
direct_costs: W-2 expediter/coordinator labor, $300k+ CGL insurance naming the City, software, travel/parking.
contribution_profit_note: At hypothesized fees and ~5-15 staff hours per plan-based permit, ~$300-$2,000 contribution per permit [E].
working_capital_note: Invoiced per milestone, likely net-30 from architects/GCs; expediter may advance City permit fees and rebill (float risk) [E].
sales_cycle: Days-weeks for one permit; months to earn repeat relationships with architects/developers.
repeat_purchase: recurring-relationship: developers, chains and sign companies file many permits per year
acquisition_channels: Mine public permit records for high-volume owners/architects/GCs without an expediter [A, WS10-S010]
Construction managers of out-of-town retail/restaurant chains
customer_accessibility: Every permit lists contacts, so buyers are identifiable from open data; but incumbents hold long relationships and buyers need confidence in DOB process knowledge.
supplier_accessibility: Labor-based; experienced licensed expediters exist (204 active names) and could be hired as employees - assumed, unverified.
competitive_intensity: moderate: fragmented (204 names; top 10 = 46%) but relationship-driven [A, WS10-S010]
entry_strategy: Focus on underserved segments (out-of-town chains, 2-6 unit developers, ADU conversions, sign permits); sell speed SLAs and live status dashboards built on public permit data; hire one experienced expediter as employee from day one.
licenses: BACP expediter company license (MCC 4-6-250) plus individual expediter licence per filer (4-6-260); fingerprinting; >=$300,000 per-occurrence CGL naming the City; disqualified for fraud/bribery convictions; age 18+ [B, WS10-S009; A, WS10-S008]. Licence fee and processing time MISSING. Exempt from 'expediter' definition: licensed architects/engineers, the GC and licensed trade contractor on their own permits [B, WS10-S009].
regulatory_barriers: Strict false-statement/anti-bribery rules; ongoing Chicago Construction Codes Modernization (Phase 3 implementation Oct 2026 per DOB alerts) [A, WS10-S004] changes procedures; City self-service portals could reduce need.
operational_risks: Application errors cause rejections and reputation damage; review times outside the firm's control; key-person dependence on an experienced expediter.
financial_risks: Low: receivable delays and permit-fee float.
geographic_constraints: Licence and know-how are City-of-Chicago specific; each suburb has separate processes.
founder_expertise: Chicago Construction Codes administrative provisions, zoning basics, DOB e-Plan/Dynamic Portal workflows, correction handling; relationship selling to architects/GCs.
staffing: Founder + 1 experienced expediter (W-2) at launch; add coordinators as volume grows (assume ~300-500 permits per coordinator-year [E]).
automation_potential: AI: checklist completeness checks, document assembly, drafting correction responses, automated status monitoring from open data, client updates. Human: code/zoning judgment, City meetings, relationships. Real but moderate savings.
delegation_potential: Good: expediting is a standard employee role; SOP-friendly; founder can own sales.
scalability: Capped by Chicago permit volume (32,032 in 2025, down from 48,540 in 2019; 29,067 in 2026 through late Nov) [A, WS10-S010]; even the busiest expediter handled ~1,000 permits.
expansion: Suburban permit services; owner's-rep services (WS10-035); zoning/ADU feasibility packages; BACP business-licence expediting; permit-data products (WS10-006).
roic_note: Capital at risk <$15k; if $60-200k operating profit is reached, ROIC is several hundred percent [E].
critical_assumptions: Private-market fees of $500-$3,000 per plan-based permit [E]
A new firm can win 150-300 permits/yr by year 3 against relationship incumbents
An experienced licensed expediter can be hired at ~$55-75k [E]
unanswered_questions: BACP expediter company licence fee and processing time
Actual private fee schedules by permit type
Share of expediter-listed permits filed by in-house staff of architects/developers vs independent firms
Effect of 2026 code-modernization on filing complexity
failure_modes: Fee compression as architects self-file with better portals/AI
Permit volumes keep falling in the 7%+ mortgage-rate environment
score_rationale: fcf 4: local ceiling and unknown fees. roic 8: <$15k capital. access 5: buyers identifiable from open data but relationship-gated. scale 3: one city, shrinking permit base. ai 6: genuine document/correction automation.
preliminary_verdict: advance - A-level open data shows ~6,400 expediter-listed permits/yr in a fragmented field; must verify private fee levels next.

title: Outsourced quantity takeoff & estimating for specialty subcontractors (remote, AI-assisted)
product_service: Per-bid quantity takeoffs and priced estimates (drywall, paint, flooring, concrete, roofing, electrical device counts) from bid PDFs, delivered in 24-72 hours; monthly retainer for a set bid volume.
target_customer: Owners/estimators of specialty subcontractors with ~$1-20M revenue that bid many jobs and lack estimating staff.
purchase_motivation: Subs win a small share of bids, so estimating labor per win is high; owners are the bottleneck; faster turnaround lets them bid more.
spending_evidence: Large fragmented buyer base: 515,720 US specialty-trade employer establishments averaging $2.49M receipts; Illinois 18,900 [C, WS10-S022]. Direct evidence of outsourced-estimating spend and prices MISSING (search budget exhausted before pricing research).
representative_operators: Remote/offshore estimating services and AI takeoff software vendors exist; names, sizes and prices not verified in this session [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per takeoff fee by sheet count/trade, or monthly subscription for N takeoffs.
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis $200-$800 per trade takeoff or $1,500-$5,000/month retainer [E].
direct_costs: Estimator labor (US or offshore), takeoff software licences, AI/API costs, QA review.
contribution_profit_note: A $400 takeoff needing ~3 estimator-hours at $25-40/hr loaded leaves ~$280-$325 [E].
working_capital_note: Retainers billable in advance; per-job fees paid on delivery by card/ACH; negligible inventory.
sales_cycle: Short (days-weeks) once trust is established via a free/sample takeoff.
acquisition_channels: Public bid lists and plan-holder lists (named subs bidding public work)
Supplier partnerships (distributors offer takeoff to contractor customers)
customer_accessibility: Many buyers with frequent need, identifiable via public bid documents; trust in accuracy is the hurdle.
supplier_accessibility: Estimator labor available remotely (assumed); software tools commercially available (assumed).
competitive_intensity: high: offshore estimating shops and self-serve AI takeoff software compete on price [E]
entry_strategy: Pick 1-2 trades, guarantee turnaround and accuracy (credit for errors), publish trade-specific assemblies; sell to subs in a few metros, then nationally.
licenses: No licence for takeoff/estimating (not engineering); general business registration; E&O insurance prudent [E].
regulatory_barriers: Minimal; liability for estimating errors is contractual.
operational_risks: Accuracy errors lose bids or cause money-losing wins; turnaround spikes at bid deadlines; scope-reading skill is scarce.
financial_risks: Low capital; main risk is error liability and churn.
geographic_constraints: None; remote delivery nationally; local pricing data needed for priced estimates.
founder_expertise: Blueprint reading, trade scopes, assemblies and unit pricing for chosen trades; QA processes.
staffing: Founder + 1-3 trained estimators by year 2; QA lead.
automation_potential: High: AI-assisted area/count extraction from PDFs, spec parsing, assembly mapping. Human: scope interpretation, exclusions, QA, pricing judgment. Risk: the same AI lets subs self-serve, eroding the service.
delegation_potential: Good: estimator role is standard and trainable; QA can be delegated.
scalability: National market; scales with estimators; commoditization pressure limits margin.
expansion: Bid-management outsourcing, submittal prep (WS10-003), supplier-sponsored takeoff programs, estimating for GCs.
roic_note: Asset-light; <$10k capital; ROIC very high if demand exists [E].
critical_assumptions: Subs will pay $200-$800 per takeoff or retainers [E]
AI tools cut takeoff hours enough to beat offshore pricing
Accuracy can be maintained without trade experience
unanswered_questions: Market prices of outsourced takeoffs by trade
Share of subs that already outsource or use AI takeoff software
Churn rates of estimating-service customers
score_rationale: entry 3: crowded and software can substitute. ai 7: AI materially cuts takeoff labor at ordinary API prices, but also arms competitors. fcf 4: unverified pricing.
preliminary_verdict: advance - cheap to validate with sample takeoffs from public bid sets; key risk is commoditization by software.

title: Submittal & closeout documentation packaging for commercial subcontractors
product_service: Assembling product-data submittals against specifications, tracking submittal logs, and compiling closeout packages (O&M manuals, warranties, as-built markups, attic stock lists) for subs on commercial projects.
target_customer: Project managers/owners of MEP and specialty subs ($3-50M revenue) on commercial work; occasionally GCs.
purchase_motivation: Closeout documents gate final payment and retainage release (up to 10% until 50% complete, 5% after, on private Illinois contracts) [A, WS10-S029]; PMs are overloaded; rejected submittals delay work.
spending_evidence: Indirect: commercial MEP demand strong (Comfort Systems backlog $11.94B vs $5.99B a year earlier) [B, WS10-S023]; large incumbents run in-house coordinators [A, WS10-S024]. Direct evidence that subs pay outsiders for this MISSING.
representative_operators: Mostly in-house project coordinators; dedicated outsourced closeout providers not identified in this session [E]
revenue_mechanism: Fixed fee per project package or per-submittal pricing; monthly retainer for a sub's active projects.
working_capital_note: Subs themselves face pay-when-paid and retainage, so expect net-45-60 payment unless prepaid [E].
sales_cycle: 1-3 months; must prove reliability on one project.
acquisition_channels: Outreach to MEP/specialty subs listed on public bid results
customer_accessibility: Subs identifiable; but outsourcing this task is not an established purchase category (unverified).
competitive_intensity: low-moderate as a service category; main competitor is in-house staff [E]
entry_strategy: Pitch as 'retainage acceleration': close out faster and get paid sooner; per-project pricing with SLA.
operational_risks: Spec interpretation errors; dependence on sub's PM responsiveness.
founder_expertise: Commercial construction specs (CSI divisions), submittal/closeout norms, PM software (Procore etc.).
automation_potential: High: AI matching spec sections to product data, assembling manuals, tracking logs. Human: client coordination, judgment on substitutions.
expansion: Bid support (WS10-002), compliance paperwork, lien/payment admin (WS10-004).
critical_assumptions: Subs will pay outsiders for closeout work
Faster closeout measurably accelerates retainage release
unanswered_questions: Do subs outsource closeout today, at what price?
Typical retainage release delay after substantial completion
failure_modes: Buyers treat it as clerical and keep it in-house
Low ticket with high coordination cost
score_rationale: access 4: unproven purchase category. ai 7: document assembly is very automatable. fcf 3: small tickets.
preliminary_verdict: hold - plausible AI-leveraged service but no evidence buyers pay for it; test via interviews later (not now).

title: Lien-rights & payment-compliance administration for Illinois subcontractors and suppliers
product_service: Tracking Illinois notice deadlines per job, preparing preliminary notices, collecting sworn statements and lien waivers, deadline alerts and payment follow-up; lien recording handled through a partner attorney.
target_customer: Small/mid subs and material suppliers (lumber yards, electrical/plumbing distributors) selling on credit to contractors.
purchase_motivation: Non-payment risk under pay-when-paid; Illinois sub notice windows (90 days after last work; 60 days from start on owner-occupied single-family) and 4-month recording deadline [C, WS10-S030]; retainage withholding [A, WS10-S029].
spending_evidence: National lien-rights software/services exist (Levelset; ownership/terms not verified) [E]; Illinois-specific spend MISSING.
representative_operators: Levelset (construction payment/lien software; cited for Illinois deadlines) [C, WS10-S030]
revenue_mechanism: Per-notice fee or monthly subscription by job volume; referral of lien filings to attorneys (fee splitting with non-lawyers is restricted - must be structured carefully).
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis $30-$100 per notice; $300-$1,500/month per active supplier [E].
working_capital_note: Subscription billed monthly in advance; negligible inventory.
sales_cycle: 1-2 months; credit managers at suppliers are the natural buyers.
customer_accessibility: Suppliers identifiable; established software competitors already sell to them.
supplier_accessibility: Requires an attorney partner for lien recording and legal advice.
competitive_intensity: high: national software platforms and law firms [E]
entry_strategy: Illinois-only depth (Chicago + Cook County recording specifics), done-for-you service rather than software.
licenses: No specific licence for administrative tracking; preparing/recording lien claims for others may constitute unauthorized practice of law in Illinois - legal review required [E].
regulatory_barriers: Unauthorized-practice-of-law boundary; rules on lawyer fee-sharing.
operational_risks: A missed deadline destroys a client's lien rights (high liability).
geographic_constraints: Illinois law-specific; expansion needs state-by-state rules.
founder_expertise: Illinois Mechanics Lien Act, Prompt Payment Act, credit management.
automation_potential: AI/software: deadline computation, document generation, waiver tracking; human: legal judgment, disputes.
scalability: Regional; software-like recurring revenue but crowded.
expansion: Collections (WS02 cross-stream), credit reports on contractors, closeout support.
critical_assumptions: A compliant structure exists that avoids UPL
Suppliers prefer done-for-you service over software
unanswered_questions: Illinois rules on non-lawyers preparing lien notices vs lien claims
Current statute text after P.A. 103-0827
score_rationale: resilience 7: demand rises when payment slows (counter-cyclical). entry 3: established software. feasibility 5: UPL boundary.
preliminary_verdict: hold - counter-cyclical need, but crowded and legally delicate; better as an add-on than a standalone first business.

title: GPR concrete scanning & private utility locating for contractors and facilities
product_service: Ground-penetrating-radar scanning of slabs/walls to locate rebar, post-tension tendons and conduit before coring/saw-cutting; locating private underground utilities on campuses and industrial sites that public one-call does not mark; marked-up reports.
target_customer: Electrical, plumbing, mechanical and low-voltage subs doing renovations; GCs; facility managers of hospitals, universities, industrial plants.
purchase_motivation: Striking a PT tendon or live conduit causes injury, outage and costly repairs; GCs/owners often require scanning before coring.
spending_evidence: Renovation volume proxy: 5,505 renovation/alteration permits in Chicago in 2025 [A, WS10-S010]; direct scanning spend and price data MISSING.
representative_operators: National scanning firms and local surveyors operate (names/sizes not verified in this session) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Half-day/full-day rates or per-scan fees; mobilization fees; emergency surcharges.
direct_costs: Technician labor, vehicle, equipment depreciation, insurance (CGL + professional).
contribution_profit_note: ~$300-$1,200 per technician-day after labor and vehicle at hypothesized rates [E].
working_capital_note: B2B net-30 typical; small jobs can be card-paid on site [E].
sales_cycle: Short: subs book scans days ahead; first trust via one successful job.
repeat_purchase: recurring-relationship: active renovation subs need scans repeatedly
acquisition_channels: Electrical/plumbing subs pulling renovation permits (open data)
customer_accessibility: Frequent-need buyers identifiable from permit data; short cycle; referrals common [E].
supplier_accessibility: GPR and EM locator equipment commercially available (assumed); training from manufacturers.
competitive_intensity: moderate: national scanning firms plus local operators [E]
entry_strategy: Fast-response coverage of downtown/near-north high-rise renovation market (PT slabs), same-day reports, flat transparent pricing.
licenses: No specific Illinois licence identified for GPR scanning (assumption to verify); CGL/E&O insurance; Chicago GC licence likely not required since no construction work performed (verify) [E].
operational_risks: Mis-reads cause strikes and claims; technician skill and retention.
financial_risks: Equipment capex $20-45k per unit [E]; liability claims.
geographic_constraints: Local service radius per technician; replicable metro by metro.
founder_expertise: GPR operation and interpretation, concrete construction basics, safety culture.
staffing: Founder as first technician; hire technicians at ~1 per $250-350k revenue [E].
automation_potential: Moderate: AI-assisted radargram interpretation, automated report generation, scheduling; field work stays human.
delegation_potential: Good: technician role trainable in weeks-months.
expansion: Concrete X-ray partnerships, utility mapping for campuses, leak detection, as-built mapping.
critical_assumptions: Enough recurring demand from renovation subs in Chicago
unanswered_questions: Market rates for GPR scanning in Chicago
Competitor count locally
Insurance cost for scanning liability
score_rationale: access 6: frequent-need B2B buyers via permit data. roic 6: modest equipment capex. evidence weak (E) on prices.
preliminary_verdict: advance - low-capital, unlicensed, repeat B2B service tied to renovation activity; validate pricing and competitor density.

title: Permit- and violation-data lead intelligence for Chicago-area contractors and suppliers
product_service: Weekly filtered, enriched lists from municipal permit and violation open data (e.g., new roofing/tuckpointing permits, porch/masonry violations, new-construction starts) delivered to subs, suppliers and service firms.
target_customer: Roofers, masonry/porch contractors, window/gutter firms, material suppliers, insurance agents for contractors.
purchase_motivation: Find jobs earlier than competitors; target buildings with active code violations.
spending_evidence: Data scale: 32,032 Chicago permits (2025) and 50,099 violations at 10,787 addresses (2025) published openly [A, WS10-S010; A, WS10-S011]. Willingness to pay MISSING; national construction-lead databases exist (not verified here) [E].
representative_operators: National construction lead/bid databases (names not verified in this session) [E]
acquisition_channels: Direct outreach to contractors appearing in permit data
customer_accessibility: Contractors identifiable, but many cheap or free alternatives (they can query open data themselves).
supplier_accessibility: Open data confirmed accessible via Socrata API [A, WS10-S010].
competitive_intensity: high: free open data plus national databases [E]
entry_strategy: Hyper-local enrichment (owner contact via property records, violation severity scoring) that contractors cannot easily do themselves.
licenses: None; customers' outreach must comply with TCPA/CAN-SPAM; owner data use subject to privacy rules [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low; privacy/robocall rules for downstream use.
geographic_constraints: Needs municipalities with open data; Chicago strong, suburbs vary.
automation_potential: High: pipeline, enrichment and scoring are fully automatable at low cost.
scalability: Limited by local willingness to pay; multi-city requires per-city data work.
expansion: Feeds WS10-010/014/032 own lead generation; national multi-city data product (WS09 cross-stream).
critical_assumptions: Contractors pay for convenience on top of free data
unanswered_questions: Competing local lead services and their pricing
score_rationale: fcf 2: low ceiling. Better as an internal lead engine for a contracting business than as a product.
preliminary_verdict: hold - weak standalone, but a valuable internal customer-acquisition tool for code-driven contracting records.

title: Commercial firestopping subcontractor (code-required penetration & joint sealing)
subindustry: Specialty trade - firestopping / passive fire protection
product_service: Installing tested firestop systems at penetrations and joints in fire-rated assemblies in new commercial/multifamily buildings and renovations; firestop surveys and remediation for existing buildings.
target_customer: GCs and MEP subs on commercial, healthcare, data-center and 5+ unit residential projects; building owners/facility managers for remediation.
purchase_motivation: Code-required rated assemblies; failed inspections stop occupancy; owners must maintain rated assemblies under IFC/NFPA 101 [C, WS10-S034].
spending_evidence: Specialty-trade economics: NAICS 238990 proxy operating margin 18.2% (2022) [C, WS10-S022]; multifamily 5+ starts +17.1% y/y (Oct 2026) [C, WS10-S020]; commercial MEP backlogs at record levels (Comfort Systems $11.94B) [B, WS10-S023]. Firestop-specific spend MISSING.
representative_operators: Specialty firestop contractors holding FM 4991 or UL Qualified Firestop Contractor status (FCIA members) [C, WS10-S034]
Large MEP incumbents (Comfort Systems GM 24.1%; EMCOR GM 19.3%) - incumbent economics [B, WS10-S023; A, WS10-S024]
revenue_mechanism: Lump-sum or unit-price subcontracts; T&M for remediation; survey fees.
direct_costs: Field labor, firestop materials (sealants, collars, wraps), lifts/rentals, insurance, documentation.
contribution_profit_note: Census 238990 proxy op margin 18% (incumbent average) [C, WS10-S022]; new entrant likely 8-15% after overhead [E].
working_capital_note: Retainage up to 10% then 5% on private jobs [A, WS10-S029]; pay-when-paid clauses; 60-90 day receivables; a $1.5M revenue firm may carry $250-400k receivables+retainage [E]; bonding may be needed on public work (SBA guarantees up to $9M non-federal) [A, WS10-S031].
acquisition_channels: MEP subs who prefer to subcontract firestopping
customer_accessibility: Reachable via standard GC prequal and bidding; credibility and insurance limits required.
supplier_accessibility: Firestop manufacturers distribute through specialty distributors (assumed accessible).
competitive_intensity: moderate: specialized niche, but MEP subs and insulation contractors also self-perform [E]
entry_strategy: Certification (FM 4991/UL QFC) as credibility signal; digital as-installed documentation (photo per penetration) that eases inspection; target renovation/remediation where incumbents are less focused.
licenses: Chicago: GC license covers most construction/repair incl. permit-exempt work; Class E $300/yr for projects <=$500k with $1M/occurrence CGL, Class D $900 ($4M projects, $2M CGL), no exam listed, financial-solvency statement required [A, WS10-S004]. Subcontractors working under a licensed GC need no own GC license [A, WS10-S004]. Residential work: Illinois Home Repair and Remodeling Act consumer rules (written contract + consumer-rights brochure over $1,000) [A, WS10-S001]. Suburbs: municipal contractor registration varies (MISSING). Firestop contractor quality programs (FM 4991, UL QFC, IAS AC291) are voluntary credentials [C, WS10-S034].
regulatory_barriers: Union labor prevalence on large Chicago commercial jobs (UNVERIFIED) may exclude non-union subs; prevailing wage on public work.
operational_risks: Installation errors found at inspection; high documentation burden; labor recruitment with no founder trade background.
financial_risks: Receivable and retainage float; GC insolvency; back-charges.
founder_expertise: Firestop systems/UL listings, code basics, estimating, GC relationships, safety programs.
staffing: Hire experienced firestop foreman early; 2-6 installers by year 2; estimator/PM.
automation_potential: Moderate: AI-assisted takeoff of penetrations, system selection from listings, automated documentation/photo logs; installation stays manual.
delegation_potential: Moderate-good: foreman/PM structure common in trades.
scalability: Regional crews; adjacencies into fire-rated door/joint inspection.
expansion: Firestop surveys/annual inspections for owners, fire-door inspections (WS05 cross), smoke-barrier remediation.
roic_note: Capital mostly working capital ($50-150k by year 2-3) [E]; ROIC ~75-200% if margins hold [E].
critical_assumptions: Non-union firm can win enough work
unanswered_questions: Union jurisdiction over firestopping in Chicago
Firestop subcontract pricing per penetration
Local special-inspection requirements under Chicago Construction Codes
failure_modes: Cash squeeze from retainage and slow pay
score_rationale: resilience 6: code-mandated but tied to construction volume. cash 3: retainage + pay-when-paid. access 4: GC prequal walls for a newcomer.
preliminary_verdict: advance - code-driven specialty with certification moat; next check union jurisdiction, pricing and GC prequal norms.

direct_costs: Sealer/crack filler/paint, seasonal labor, fuel, equipment depreciation.
contribution_profit_note: Material is a modest share; contribution 40-55% in season [E].
working_capital_note: Commercial net-30; some HOAs pay deposits; seasonal (May-Oct in Chicago) so winter cash buffer needed [E].
repeat_purchase: recurring: 2-3 year sealcoat cycle; annual crack fill/striping
customer_accessibility: Property managers reachable; vendor onboarding required; price-shopping common.
supplier_accessibility: Sealer and equipment widely available from regional distributors (assumed).
competitive_intensity: high: low barrier, many small operators [E]
entry_strategy: Satellite-measured instant proposals, multi-site program pricing for portfolio managers, reliable scheduling.
licenses: Chicago: GC license covers most construction/repair incl. permit-exempt work; Class E $300/yr for projects <=$500k with $1M/occurrence CGL, Class D $900 ($4M projects, $2M CGL), no exam listed, financial-solvency statement required [A, WS10-S004]. Subcontractors working under a licensed GC need no own GC license [A, WS10-S004]. regulatory_barriers: Coal-tar sealant bans in some jurisdictions (unverified locally); ADA striping standards.
operational_risks: Weather windows; seasonal labor; quality complaints.
founder_expertise: Pavement maintenance methods, estimating, crew management.

automation_potential: Moderate: satellite measurement and AI-generated proposals, routing; work manual.
scalability: Add rigs; seasonal ceiling; adjacency into snow removal (WS05/WS18) for year-round use.

critical_assumptions: Enough commercial contracts can be won against low-price incumbents
unanswered_questions: Chicago-area pricing per sq ft
Licensing treatment of sealcoating in Chicago
score_rationale: Workable but crowded seasonal trade; overlap with WS05 parking-lot maintenance.
preliminary_verdict: hold - realistic cash business with seasonal ceiling; WS05 likely covers it more fully.

title: Post-construction (rough/final/touch-up) cleaning for GCs and developers
product_service: Rough, final and touch-up cleaning phases before inspection/turnover of new and renovated commercial and multifamily space; debris removal coordination.
target_customer: GCs, multifamily developers, restoration contractors, commercial tenant build-out contractors.

representative_operators: Commercial cleaning firms with construction divisions; specialist post-construction cleaners (not verified) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-square-foot by phase or lump sum per project.
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis $0.10-$0.40 per sq ft per project [E].
direct_costs: Labor, supplies, lifts for high windows, insurance.
